title: Uniform Discrete Diffusion with Metric Path for Video Generation

response.summary: URSA applies uniform discrete flow matching to visual tokens, combining an embedding-distance probability path, resolution-dependent timestep shifting, and frame-wise asynchronous noise schedules. The resulting 1.7B model reports competitive image/video benchmark results, but the methodological novelty is incremental and several central scalability and multitask claims are insufficiently validated.
strengths: The work tackles an important gap between discrete-token and continuous video generators with a conceptually simple global-refinement framework (pp. 2–6).
URSA is evaluated across text-to-video, image-to-video, and text-to-image benchmarks and is competitive among discrete methods despite its relatively modest parameter count (pp. 7–8).
Sampling-step, path-schedule, model-size, and timestep-shift studies provide some useful empirical characterization (pp. 8–10).
weaknesses: The main components substantially inherit prior ideas—metric-induced discrete paths from Shaul et al. and asynchronous scheduling from diffusion forcing—while the claimed linearized path is largely hyperparameter calibration by visual inspection; the precise new technical contribution is therefore limited (pp. 5–7).

Core evidence is incomplete: there is no controlled ablation of asynchronous scheduling, no convincing resolution-dependent study across sequence lengths, and no quantitative evaluation of interpolation, extrapolation, or minute-long generation despite these being headline claims (pp. 2, 5, 9–10).

Reproducibility and comparison fairness are weak: the velocity/sampling construction is deferred to an absent Appendix A, important architecture/data-curation details are underspecified, 12M internal videos are used, and training data include 14M FLUX-generated images, complicating comparisons against FLUX and other models (pp. 6–8).
response.score_rationale: The competitive discrete-generation results and broad benchmark coverage are promising, but they do not yet establish the paper's strongest scalability and unified-task claims. Incremental novelty, missing core ablations, absent promised sampling details, and data/comparison confounds place the work marginally below the acceptance bar. Some uncertainty remains because qualitative video behavior cannot be fully assessed from static figures.

response.summary: URSA applies uniform discrete flow matching to visual tokens, combining an embedding-distance probability path, resolution-dependent timestep shifting, and frame-wise asynchronous noise schedules. The resulting 1.7B model is empirically competitive on several image/video benchmarks, but the claimed novelty and breadth are not fully substantiated by controlled experiments or sufficient methodological detail.
strengths: Strong empirical performance for a relatively small discrete model: 82.4 VBench text-to-video, 86.2 VBench++ image-to-video, and 86.0 DPG-Bench at 1024×1024 (pp. 7–8).

The global iterative-refinement formulation is well motivated for reducing discrete generation errors, and the inference-step study shows consistent gains over masked diffusion and a mixture-path variant, especially for video (pp. 8–9).
A single framework supports image, video, and conditional generation, with useful scaling and scheduler studies (pp. 9–10).
weaknesses: The components appear largely adapted from prior work: the metric path and solver follow Shaul et al., timestep shifting is attributed to continuous diffusion practice, and asynchronous scheduling follows Diffusion Forcing; the paper does not sharply isolate its novel technical contribution (pp. 5–6, 10).

Evidence does not adequately support several central claims. Minute-level generation, interpolation, extrapolation, and unified multitask ability lack quantitative evaluation; the supplied paper contains no referenced appendices, and even Figure 1 shows only a 40-second example (pp. 1–2, 5–6).

Comparisons are heavily confounded by architecture, training data, tokenizer, prompt rewriting, and compute. Training includes 24M videos with 12M internal pairs and 14M FLUX-generated images, while there are no matched-data or matched-compute baselines; the resolution-dependent shift and asynchronous schedule also lack direct ablations (pp. 6–10).
response.score_rationale: The work is promising and empirically strong, but currently sits marginally below acceptance because its main ingredients are incremental integrations and the decisive long-video/multitask claims are insufficiently evaluated. Missing sampling details and absent appendices further limit reproducibility. I would raise the score with controlled component ablations and quantitative long-duration and conditional-generation evidence.

response.summary: URSA applies uniform discrete diffusion to image/video tokens, combining an embedding-distance probability path, resolution-dependent timestep shifting, and frame-wise asynchronous corruption. The reported benchmark results are strong, but the methodological novelty is largely an integration of existing discrete flow matching, timestep shifting, and diffusion-forcing ideas, while essential algorithmic and long-video evidence is missing.
strengths: Strong empirical results for a relatively small 1.7B discrete model across text-to-video, image-to-video, and text-to-image benchmarks (pp. 7–8).
The global iterative-refinement formulation is practically appealing and appears more step-efficient than masked diffusion, especially for video (pp. 8–9, Fig. 4).
The paper studies path parameters, model scaling, and timestep shifting rather than reporting only final-system performance (pp. 9–10).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the metric scheduler is based on Kinetic Optimal Scheduling, asynchronous scheduling follows Diffusion Forcing, and the timestep shift is attributed to prior continuous diffusion work (pp. 5–6, 10). The main contribution is therefore system-level integration and scaling.

Technical specification is incomplete and sometimes imprecise: Eq. 3 is malformed, the stated condition does not establish that d is a metric, and the velocity/sampling update is deferred to Appendix A, yet the supplied manuscript ends at the references without any appendices (pp. 5–6, 16).

Evidence does not substantiate several central claims: there is no controlled ablation of asynchronous scheduling, no quantitative long-duration or multitask evaluation, and cross-model comparisons use heterogeneous data, resolutions, and prompt rewriting; 12M internal videos further limit reproducibility (pp. 6–8).
response.score_rationale: The work has meaningful engineering value and competitive results, placing it near the acceptance boundary. However, limited algorithmic novelty, missing promised appendices and sampling details, and inadequate evidence for the asynchronous and minute-long-generation claims outweigh the empirical strengths. Confidence is fairly high, though assessment of visual quality is uncertain without videos or the absent appendices.

response.summary: URSA applies uniform discrete flow matching to visual tokens, combining an embedding-distance probability path, timestep shifting, and frame-wise asynchronous noise schedules. The reported discrete-generation results are promising, but the methodological novelty is largely a combination of prior mechanisms, key technical and implementation details are missing, and several broad claims—especially minute-long generation and unified multitask capability—lack quantitative support.
strengths: Strong empirical performance for a relatively small discrete model: URSA reaches 82.4 VBench with 1.7B parameters and improves substantially over listed discrete video baselines (pp. 7–8).
The inference-step and path ablations provide useful evidence that global iterative refinement and the metric path improve discrete image/video generation (pp. 8–9).
The framework covers text-to-image, text-to-video, and zero-shot image-to-video generation within a common token-based architecture (pp. 7–8).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the metric-induced path and Euler sampling are adopted from Shaul et al., timestep shifting is attributed to continuous diffusion practice, and asynchronous scheduling follows Diffusion Forcing (pp. 5–6, 10); the paper does not clearly isolate a new technical principle beyond their combination.

Technical specification is incomplete and sometimes imprecise: Eq. 3 is malformed and calls d a metric while stating only identity of indiscernibles; the velocity construction and complete sampling algorithm are deferred to an absent Appendix A, and no explicit resolution-to-shift rule is given (pp. 4–6).

Evidence does not substantiate several headline claims: there is no quantitative evaluation of interpolation, extrapolation, or minute-long videos, despite references to absent Appendices C/D; I2V performance is below several specialized models, and comparisons are confounded by prompt rewriting, tokenizer differences, large synthetic/proprietary datasets, and limited controlled ablations (pp. 6–10).
response.score_rationale: The work demonstrates meaningful empirical progress for discrete video generation, but the incremental synthesis of existing techniques, incomplete technical presentation, and weak evidence for its broad long-video and multitask claims place it below the acceptance threshold. Uncertainty remains because the referenced appendices and fuller qualitative videos are not present in the supplied manuscript.

response.summary: URSA adapts uniform discrete flow matching to visual tokens using an embedding-distance path, resolution-dependent timestep shifting, and frame-wise asynchronous noise schedules. The reported image/video benchmark results are strong, but the methodological novelty is incremental and several central claims lack adequate specification or evidence.
strengths: Strong results for a relatively compact 1.7B discrete model, including 82.4 VBench and 86.0 DPG-Bench (pp. 7–8).
The iterative-refinement study compares masked diffusion, mixture-path uniform diffusion, and the proposed metric path across inference budgets, showing especially clear video gains (pp. 8–9).
A single framework is presented for text-to-image, text-to-video, and frame-conditioned generation, with competitive I2V results despite no task-specific adaptation being reported (pp. 5, 7–8).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method explicitly adopts prior discrete flow matching/Kinetic Optimal Scheduler and Euler sampling, while asynchronous scheduling follows diffusion forcing and timestep shifting follows continuous diffusion practice (pp. 5–7, 10). The distinct technical contribution is therefore mainly path calibration.

Key claims are insufficiently supported. There is no ablation of asynchronous scheduling, no quantitative evaluation of interpolation/extrapolation or minute-level generation, and no demonstrated rule connecting resolution to the shift parameter; some headline claims also overstate the tables, since multiple continuous models exceed URSA on VBench and VBench++ (pp. 7–10).

Reproducibility and soundness are weakened by missing details: the cited Appendices A/C/D are absent from the supplied manuscript, sampling velocities and conditioning procedures are not specified, the path parameters are selected by visual inspection, and Eq. 3 has ambiguous softmax/product notation and calls a distance a metric without stating the full metric conditions (pp. 4–6).
response.score_rationale: The paper offers useful empirical evidence that metric-path discrete refinement can be competitive, but the core components are close to existing techniques and decisive claims about versatile and long-form generation are not validated. Missing appendices and underspecified sampling further prevent confident verification, placing it marginally below acceptance.
